draft.title: Structure and pace
card: Pace is how fast or slow a text feels to read. A writer controls it through structure: how the text is built and ordered.
Short paragraphs and short sentences speed a reader up. Long, detailed paragraphs slow the reader down.
A scene break lets a writer skip time, such as a week or a year, in a line or two. This moves the story along quickly.
A writer can stretch a tense moment by describing each second in detail. This makes the reader feel the tension for longer.
draft.remember: Structure sets pace: the way a writer builds and orders the text shapes how fast it feels and what the reader feels.

a.q: A story spends a full page on the three seconds before Jai opens an exam result. What is the effect on the reader?
opts: It slows the pace and stretches the tension
It speeds the pace and hurries the reader on
It skips time and moves the story ahead
It makes the moment feel unimportant
a.why: Spending a lot of text on a very short moment slows the pace, so the reader feels the tension for longer. It does not hurry the reader, because long detailed writing slows reading down.
a.clue: Think about how much text is given to how little time.

b.q: A writer ends a scene with Mina waving goodbye at the airport. The next scene begins: 'Three years later, the letter arrived.' What does this scene break do?
opts: It skips time and quickens the pace
It slows time to build tension
It describes one moment in close detail
It repeats an earlier event for emphasis
b.why: The scene break jumps across three years in a single line, so the story moves on quickly. It does not slow the story, because no moment is stretched or described in detail.
b.clue: Count how much time passes and how many words it takes.

a.best: It slows the pace and stretches the tension

b.best: It skips time and quickens the pace
